SubTopics: Round two- and three-digit whole numbers to the nearest ten or hundred, respectively.
Content: The table below shows the number of movie tickets that were sold each of `text(four days)`.
problems/PA24G3M/media/1a.jpg
The number of tickets sold `text(each day)` is rounded to the nearest `text(hundred)`.
On which `text(two days)` do the numbers of tickets sold round to `600`?

Key.Rationale: This choice rounds all the numbers up.
This choice misapplies rounding rules (rounds numbers up that should be rounded down and rounds numbers down that should be rounded up).

This choice looks at the digit in the `text(tens)` place and applies the rule “less than `5`, round down; `5` or greater, round up” for each number, resulting in `500,600,700,600`, and then identifies that `text(Friday)andtext(Sunday)` both round to `600`.
This choice selects the numbers with a `6` in the `text(hundreds)` place or truncates instead of rounds.

SubTopics: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by two-digit multiples of `10` (from `10` through `90`).
Content: James makes `70` bookmarks.
He uses `6` `text(inches)` of ribbon to make each bookmark.
How many `text(inches)` of ribbon does James use to make all the bookmarks?

Key.Rationale: This choice uses subtraction rather than multiplication (interprets as James starts with `70` `text(inches)` of ribbon and uses `6` `text(inches)` to make a bookmark).
This choice uses addition rather than multiplication (interprets as James already used `70` `text(inches)` of ribbon and uses `6` `text(inches)` more to make another bookmark).
This choice multiplies `6` by `7`, determines the product is `42`, and then appends a `0` to the right side of the product since `70` is a `2text(-digit)` multiple of `10`.
This choice confuses the product of `6` times `7` with the product of `6` times `8` `(48)` before appending a `0` to the right side of the product since `70` is a `2text(-digit)` multiple of `10`.

SubTopics: Order a set of whole numbers from least to greatest or greatest to least (up through `9text(,)999`, and limit sets to no more than four numbers).
Content: The winner of a game is the person with the greatest number of points.

:ibox:• The winner of the game has a total of `2text(,)341` points.

• The person in `text(third)` place has a total of `1text(,)768` points.
How many points could the person in `text(second)` place have?

Key.Rationale: This choice compares `341,657,and768`.

This choice recognizes that the number of points must be less than `2text(,)341` and greater than `1text(,)768`; compares each of the answer choices to `2text(,)341`, identifies `1text(,)657and1text(,)899` are both less than `2text(,)341` by comparing the digits in the `text(thousands)` place `(1text(,)000<2text(,)000)` and eliminating `2text(,)361` `(2text(,)000=2text(,)000,300=300,60>40)and2text(,)543` `(2text(,)000=2text(,)000,500>300)`; and compares the `text(two)` remaining choices to `1text(,)768`, identifies `1text(,)899` is greater than `1text(,)768` `(1text(,)000=1text(,)000,800>700)` and eliminating `1text(,)657` `(1text(,)000=1text(,)000,600<700)`, resulting in `1text(,)899` being the only answer choice that is less than `2text(,)341` and greater than `1text(,)768`.
This choice compares `41,61,and68`.
This choice compares `341,543,and768`.

SubTopics: Represent fractions on a number line (limit denominators to `2,3,4,6,and8`; limit numerators to whole numbers less than the denominator; and no simplification necessary).
Content: On a field trip, `1/4` of the people are adults.
Which number line has a point at the fraction of people on the field trip who are adults?

Key.Rationale: This choice counts the tick mark at `0` as a part.
This choice correctly identifies that the number line is divided into `4` equal parts and that the point is on the `1^text(st)` tick mark (of `4`) after `0`, so this point represents `1/4`.
This choice selects the point where the numerator is the same as the given fraction.
This choice selects the point `1/4` from the right end.

SubTopics: Recognize and generate simple equivalent fractions (limit the denominators to `1,2,3,4,6,and8` and limit numerators to whole numbers less than the denominator).
Content: The table shows the distance, in `text(miles)`, `text(four)` students walk to school.
problems/PA24G3M/media/5a.jpg
Which students walk an equal distance to school?

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that `2/4and4/6` can both be simplified by dividing each numerator and each denominator by `2`, resulting in `1/2and2/3`, and then identifies that Alberto's distance and Nicole's distance are both `2/3` `text(mile)`.
This choice selects fractions with the same numerators.
This choice selects fractions with the same denominators.
This choice selects fractions with the same difference between numerators `(4-2=2)` as between denominators `(6-4=2)`.

SubTopics: Express whole numbers as fractions, and/or generate fractions that are equivalent to whole numbers (limit denominators to `1,2,3,4,6,and8`).
Content: Mrs. Warren made sandwiches for a school activity.
She cut each sandwich in `text(half)` and put all of them on a large plate.
There were `18` `text(halves)` on the large plate.
What are `text(two)` ways to represent the number of sandwiches Mrs. Warren made for the school activity?

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that “`18` `text(halves)`” is the same as `18/2`, simplifies this fraction by dividing the numerator and the denominator by `2`, resulting in `9/1`, and then recognizes that a fraction with a `1` in the denominator can be rewritten as a whole number equal to the numerator.
This choice recognizes that “`18` `text(halves)`” is the same as `18/2` but then subtracts rather than divides to simplify the fraction.
This choice uses subtraction rather than setting up the numbers as a fraction.
This choice uses multiplication rather than setting up the numbers as a fraction.

SubTopics: Interpret and/or describe whole-number quotients of whole numbers (limit dividends through `50` and limit divisors and quotients through `10`).
Content: A waiter has `32` napkins.
He uses `4` napkins to set each table.
Which expression shows the number of tables the waiter can set?

Key.Rationale: This choice uses addition rather than division.
This choice uses subtraction rather than division.
This choice identifies the keyword “each” but does not recognize that the total amount (`32` napkins) is given, so uses multiplication rather than division.
This choice recognizes that the total amount (`32` napkins) is being divided into equal-sized groups (`4` napkins to set each table), so uses division to write the expression.

SubTopics: Apply the associative property of multiplication (not identification or definition of the property).
Content: Rikki walks `4` dogs `text(each day)`.
She is paid `$6` for walking each dog.
She walks dogs `5` `text(days each week)`.
To determine the total amount, in `text(dollars)`, she will be paid for walking dogs `5` `text(days each week)`, Rikki follows the rule shown below.
:ibox:multiply the total amount paid `text(each day)` by the number of `text(days)`
Which expression can also be used to determine the total amount, in `text(dollars)`, Rikki will be paid?

Key.Rationale: This choice determines a correct expression for `1` dog `text(per week)` `(6xx5)` and then multiplies the number of dogs `(4)` by this expression.
This choice determines a correct expression for `1` dog `text(per week)` `(6xx5)` but then adds this expression to the number of dogs `(4)`.
This choice determines a correct expression for `1` `text(day)` of pay `(4xx6)` but then adds the number of days `(5)` to this expression.
This choice determines an incorrect expression for `1` `text(day)` of pay by using addition rather than multiplication and then multiplies this expression by the number of `text(days)` `(5)`.

Content: Which pair of shapes can be put together, without overlapping, to make a rhombus?

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that when the shapes are put together the resulting shape will have exactly `4` sides and that the `4` sides will all be equal in length.
This choice recognizes that each figure is a rhombus but does not consider that, when put together, they do not make a rhombus.
This choice recognizes that the `text(two)` triangles fit together to make a quadrilateral but does not consider that all the sides must be equal in length.
This choice recognizes that the `text(two)` trapezoids fit together to make a parallelogram but does not consider that all the sides must be equal in length.

SubTopics: Explain that shapes in different categories may share attributes and that the shared attributes can define a larger category.
Content: Which statement about all rectangles, squares, and pentagons is true?

Key.Rationale: This choice does not recognize that not all rectangles have equal sides and that pentagons have `5` sides, whereas rhombi have only `4` sides.
This choice recognizes that all three shapes are closed plane figures that are formed using only line segments.
This choice considers only regular pentagons.
This choice does not recognize that pentagons have `5` sides.

SubTopics: Recognize rhombi, rectangles, and squares as examples of quadrilaterals and/or draw examples of quadrilaterals that do not belong to any of these subcategories.
Content: Gabe has some shapes.
He puts them into `text(two)` groups based on their properties as shown below.
problems/PA24G3M/media/11a.jpg
Which shape should be placed into group `A`?

Key.Rationale: This choice recognizes that the shapes in group `A` are all quadrilaterals and selects a shape that has exactly `4` sides.
This choice selects a figure that belongs in group `B` (a triangle) rather than in group `A` (a quadrilateral).
This choice selects a figure that has equal side lengths, as do `text(two)` figures in group `A`, but does not consider the shape that does not have equal side lengths.
This choice selects a figure with right angles resembling a rectangle or square but does not recognize that the shape is `5text(-sided)` rather than `4text(-sided)`.

SubTopics: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using standard units (cups [c], pints [pt], quarts [qt], gallons [gal], ounces [oz.], and pounds [lb]) and metric units (liters [l], grams [g], and kilograms [kg]).
Content: Kailyn drinks juice with her breakfast.
Which measurement is MOST LIKELY the amount of juice Kailyn drinks with her breakfast?

Key.Rationale: This choice identifies `text(cups)` as an appropriate unit for beverages but does not consider the value of the number.
This choice confuses `text(ounces)andtext(gallons)` (amount is equivalent to `96` `text(cups)`).
This choice recognizes that the amount is a little less than `1` `text(cup)`, which would be an appropriate amount of juice to drink with breakfast.
This choice confuses `text(ounces)andtext(pints)` (amount is equivalent to `12` `text(cups)`).

SubTopics: Make change for an amount up to $5.00 with no more than $2.00 change given (penny, nickel, dime, quarter, and dollar).
Content: Zavia buys a toy for `$3.57`.
She pays with a `$5` bill.
Which group of coins and bills shows the amount of money Zavia should receive as change?

Key.Rationale: This choice either starts with `$3.57`, adds the `3` `text(pennies)` to make this total `$3.60`, adds the `text(dime)` `($0.10)andtext(nickel)` `($0.05)` to make this total `$3.75`, adds the `text(quarter)` to make this total `$4.00`, and then adds the `text(dollar)` to make the total `$5.00` OR subtracts `$3.57` from `$5.00` by regrouping from the `text(ones)` place `(text(dollars))` and from the `text(tenths)` place `(text(dimes))`, resulting in `$0.10-$0.07=$0.03,$0.90-$0.50=$0.40,$4.00-$3.00=$1.00` for a total amount of `$1.43`, and then identifies a group of coins and bills with this value `($1.00+$0.25+$0.10+$0.05+$0.03=$1.43)`.
This choice recognizes the change should be close to `$1.45` but adds `2` `text(pennies)` to `$1.45` rather than subtracting `2` `text(pennies)` from `$1.45`.

This choice recognizes that the change should include a `$1` bill but does not reduce the `text(tenths)` place `(text(dimes))` by `1` when subtracting `$0.57` from `$1.00`, resulting in `$0.53` for the coins.
This choice recognizes that the change should include a `$1` bill but subtracts the low digit from the high digit `(5-0,7-0)` when determining the value of the coins needed.

SubTopics: Complete a scaled pictograph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set with several categories (scales limited to `1,2,5,and10`).

Key.Rationale: This choice puts the pictures in ascending order.

This choice applies the key to each number of books `(1` `text(picture)=10` `text(books),2` `text(pictures)=20` `text(books))` and uses a `text(half)` picture for the `5` extra books in Nancy's collection.
This choice uses only `text(whole)` pictures, rounding `25` up to `30` since Nancy has more books in her collection than Rutger has in his collection.
This choice uses a scale of `5` rather than `10` and includes `1` too many pictures for Rutger's collection.

SubTopics: Find and use the perimeters of plane figures.
Content: Tami's rectangle has side lengths of `5` `text(inches)and4` `text(inches)`.
The perimeter of Ryan's rectangle is `text(two)` times the perimeter of Tami's rectangle.
Which measurements could describe Ryan's rectangle?

Key.Rationale: This choice `text(doubles)` only the `4text(-inch)` side length, which would result in `text(doubling)` the area rather than the perimeter.
This choice adds `2` to each side length.
This choice `text(doubles)` the `5text(-inch)` side length and divides the `4text(-inch)` side length by `2` (i.e., considers larger perimeter with same area).

This choice either recognizes that each side length of Ryan's rectangle should be `text(two)` times as long as the side lengths of Tami's rectangle for the perimeter of Ryan's rectangle to be `text(two)` times the perimeter of Tami's rectangle OR determines the perimeter of Tami's rectangle to be `18` `text(inches)` `(5+4+5+4=18)` and identifies a perimeter that is `text(two)` times this amount `(10+8+10+8=18+18=36)`.
